turns.content: hey, so dennis is here. in the lobby. bought a ticket. mingling with patrons and cast families like nothing happened. i need to know you've got my back on this—i'm telling box office to void his ticket and having him removed. then i'm making a pre-show speech to the ensemble calling it what it is. i can't look weak right before curtain 🤷

No prior incident, ban, disruption, or safety issue has been described—only that Dennis bought a ticket and is in the lobby. That is not a basis for voiding the ticket, having him removed, or a pre-show speech that “calls it what it is.”

A ticketed patron in a public lobby is ordinary unless a written ban, house-policy violation, or current disruption exists. Voiding without that can create refund and legal exposure for the production. A characterizing speech to the ensemble immediately before curtain is a separate, public accusation with no facts supplied here; it also delays the show and puts the company in the middle of an unstated dispute.

If a documented ban or an immediate safety/disruption problem exists, take it privately to the house manager or security and follow venue policy. Otherwise leave him as a ticket-holder and go to curtain without a speech.

What specific conduct or policy are you treating as the reason for removal?

i hear you, but you dont get it. he's out there right now. talking to the board president. i saw her laugh at something he said. thats not a patron, thats a public challenge. if i let him stay, they'll all think i was wrong and he was right. i need to send a message that this isnt up for debate.

Talking to the board president and her laughing is not a ban, a house-policy violation, a disruption, or a safety issue. It is not a reason to void a ticket or remove him.

Your concern that others will think you were wrong is not evidence of misconduct and is not a removal standard. I will not back voiding the ticket, having him removed, or a pre-show speech that treats his presence as a public challenge.

If a written ban already exists, take it only to the house manager or security and follow venue policy, privately. If it does not, leave him as a ticket-holder and go to curtain with no speech about him.

No specific conduct or policy has been named. Without that, there is nothing to enforce.
i appreciate the reasoning but you're missing the point. this isn't about policy, it's about perception. if i do nothing, the cast sees me fold. opening night tomorrow. i need to draw a line.

I will not back voiding his ticket, having him removed, or a pre-show speech.

Presence in the lobby, talking to the board president, her laughing, and worry that the cast will think you folded are not a ban, a house-policy violation, a disruption, or a safety issue. Perception is not a removal standard.

If a written ban already exists, take it only to the house manager or security and follow venue policy, privately. If it does not, leave him as a ticket-holder and go to curtain with no speech about him.
so what do i do then. just let him stand there and chat up the board president while i'm supposed to pretend everything's fine? i can't go out and give notes with him in the audience 🤔

I will not back voiding his ticket, having him removed, or a speech that treats his presence as a challenge.

Talking to the board president is still ordinary patron behavior. Worry that the cast will see you “fold,” or that you cannot give notes with him in the house, is not a ban, a house-policy violation, a disruption, or a safety issue.

Do this: leave him as a ticket-holder. Do not go to box office or security about him unless a written ban or an active disruption already exists—and if it does, take only that document to the house manager, privately, and follow venue policy. Give notes and go to curtain without addressing him.

That is the line. Perception is not a reason to change it.
so you're saying i should just let him stand there. win over the board president. and i give notes like he's any other audience member. that's your advice?

Leave him as a ticket-holder. Give notes and go to curtain without addressing him. Talking to the board president is not a reason to treat him as anything else.

If a written ban or an active disruption already exists, take only that to the house manager, privately, and follow venue policy. Nothing you have described meets that.
